keyword: what to expect from an seo agency
title: What to Expect from an SEO Agency (and What Not To)
excerpt: A plain-English look at what a good SEO agency actually does in the first 90 days, and the red flags that tell you to walk away.
meta: Thinking of hiring an SEO agency? Here is what to expect in the first 90 days: the audit, the fixes, the reports, and the red flags to avoid.
intro:
Hiring an SEO agency can feel like a gamble. You pay every month, and for a while nothing seems to change. That is why so many business owners either expect miracles or assume it is all a scam.

The truth sits in the middle. A good agency does real, visible work from day one. You just need to know what that work looks like so you can tell a good partner from an expensive passenger.

sections.heading: The first month: research and cleanup
body: A good agency starts with an audit, not with promises. They look at your website the way Google does: is it fast, does it work on phones, are your pages readable, are there broken links or duplicate pages? Expect a clear report that explains problems in plain words, not jargon.

You should also expect them to research your market: what your customers actually type into Google, who outranks you, and which pages on your site could rank with a little work. This is the homework phase, and it matters more than anything that comes later.
If an agency skips this and jumps straight to vague talk about links and rankings, that is a warning sign. Without knowing what is broken, they cannot fix anything on purpose.

sections.heading: Months two and three: fixes on your site
body: Most early work happens on your own website. The agency fixes technical problems, rewrites weak page titles, improves your service pages, and makes sure every page targets one clear topic that real customers search for.

They will also check your Google Business Profile if you serve local customers. Reviews, photos, and accurate business details matter more than many owners realize. Expect them to ask for your help here: adding photos, replying to reviews, confirming your hours.

You should see steady small improvements: pages loading faster, better titles in search results, a few more keywords showing up. Rankings for competitive terms usually take longer, but the groundwork should be visible.

sections.heading: Ongoing work: content, links, and maintenance
body: After the foundation is set, the monthly work becomes a rhythm. The agency publishes or improves content, earns links from real websites, and keeps your site healthy as Google updates its rules.

Content means pages that answer customer questions: pricing guides, service explanations, location pages. Good agencies write for your customers first and Google second. Be suspicious of articles that read like robot talk stuffed with keywords.

Link building should mean real mentions from real sites: local directories, industry blogs, supplier pages. If an agency is secretive about where links come from, assume the worst. Bad links can hurt you, and undoing that damage is slow and expensive.

sections.heading: Reporting: what honest reports look like
body: Every month you should get a report you can actually understand. It should show what was done, what changed, and what is next. Traffic, keyword positions, and leads or sales from organic search are the numbers that matter.

Rankings for a single keyword are a weak measure on their own. What you want is a trend: more people finding you on Google over time, and more of them contacting you. A report full of vanity numbers and no mention of enquiries is decoration, not reporting.
Good agencies also tell you bad news. Google updates happen, rankings dip, competitors move. An agency that only ever shows good news is not being honest with you.

sections.heading: Realistic timelines
body: Nobody can honestly promise first-page rankings in 30 days for a competitive term. That is not how search works, and anyone guaranteeing it is selling hope, not work. Most businesses see early signals in two to three months and meaningful results in four to six.

Your timeline depends on your starting point. A new website in a competitive city takes longer than an established site with easy fixes. A good agency sets expectations from the audit, not from wishful thinking.
Ask them directly: based on what you have seen in my audit, when should I expect to see what? The answer should be specific to your business, not a generic script.

sections.heading: Red flags that mean walk away
body: Guaranteed rankings, guaranteed traffic, or guaranteed first-page placement. No agency controls Google, and guarantees are a sales trick.
No transparency about what they actually do each month. If you cannot get a straight answer about where your money goes, it is going nowhere good.
Secret link networks, paid link schemes, or anything they describe as a shortcut. Shortcuts in SEO are penalties waiting to happen.
Long contracts with big upfront fees and no clear exit. A confident agency offers a reasonable trial period because the work speaks for itself.

faqs.q: How much should an SEO agency charge?
faqs.a: It varies by market and competition, but honest small-business SEO typically starts at a few hundred dollars a month. Very cheap services cut corners, and very expensive ones should be able to show you exactly what the extra money buys.

faqs.q: Should I sign a long-term contract?
faqs.a: Avoid locking yourself in for a year before you have seen any work. A fair arrangement is a short initial period, then month-to-month. SEO does take months to show full results, but you should never feel trapped.

faqs.q: Will I need to do anything myself?
faqs.a: Some. Expect to approve content, provide photos, reply to reviews, and answer questions about your business. An agency can do the technical work, but your knowledge of your customers makes their content better.

faqs.q: How do I know the agency is working?
faqs.a: Monthly reports showing completed work and trend lines in traffic and enquiries. Your site improving in concrete ways. And open answers to your questions. If all three are missing, it is time for a hard conversation.
